section: Modifications to the Circuits for Deployment
text:
Modifications to the Circuits for Deployment
To prepare the sensors for deployment at Dana Point, the pressure sensor and thermistor circuits were modified to more appropriately scale their predicted output range to the input range of the Teensy 4.0.

Sensor Justification
The thermistor was chosen over the IC sensor and thermocouple because of its fast response time, higher sensitivity, very low effect of lead resistance on accuracy, and ease of linearising its non-linear relationship between output resistance and temperature.The NXFT15XH103FEAB035 thermistor was chosen to collect temperature data because of its large operating temperature range (-40-125°C), high accuracy (±1% resistance), and easy integration with the AUV.
The team decided that temperature and pressure sensors would be suitable for this project’s goals because the concept of geostrophic balance would help us back-calculate debris drop locations.
Geostrophic balance describes the state of fluid flow (currents) in the ocean based on a steady-state force balance between the pressure gradient in the ocean (which is influenced by factors such as surface winds) and the apparent force on particles moving in the water relative to the Earth’s rotating reference frame. The velocity of fluid particles along the Cartesian x and y axes is related to the fluid density, Earth’s rotation rate, and the latitude of the particle. Flows in the ocean occur along lines of equal pressure, so there would be a different set of current vectors at each measured depth. The density of seawater changes throughout the ocean based on the One Atmosphere International Equation of State of Seawater, which is dependent on temperature and salinity. Salinity of ocean water is roughly constant over 10-100m of depth and along the ocean surface. However, temperature in the ocean changes rapidly (10-20°C fluctuation) over the first 400m deep into the ocean, especially in mid-latitude regions (including California). Thus, to characterize oceanic currents according to the above, pressure and temperature readings were collected at various points in the ocean.


Pressure Sensor
The MPX5700 outputs voltages that are linearly related to absolute pressure. It was expected that the pressure sensor would output voltages of 0.85-1.04V corresponding to depths of 0-3m below the ocean’s surface. The 0-3m range was chosen because Dana Point Harbour has depths between 6-15ft (1.83-4.57m), and the deployment locations were in shallower regions with a 0-3m range. As shown in Figure X, the offset amplifier (U3) was modified to scale this output to nearly fill the 0-3.3V input range of the Teensy 4.0 microcontroller to maximize data resolution. A unity gain buffer (U2) was placed between the pressure sensor and offset amplifier to prevent loading effects.



Figure X. Modified Pressure Sensor Circuit Schematic


The offset amplifier was designed with an offset of 14.56V and a gain of -14, calculated using the offset amplifier equation \(V_{out}=5\left(1+\frac{R_f}{R_{n1}}\right)\left(\frac{R_g}{R_{p1}+R_g}\right)-\frac{V_{in}R_f}{R_{n1}}\label{eq}\). The variable values in this equation for this circuit are as depicted in Figure X. This resulted in theoretical output voltages of 0.01-2.73V for depths 3-0m, which is within the desired range. A small voltage buffer was left on each side of the output to ensure fluctuations from noise and unanticipated depths slightly outside the expected range would not cause the circuit to rail out.
The output of the pressure sensor is DC voltage, so the 10Hz sampling frequency in the code was sufficient. However, as described in the P-control section, the depth control algorithm was modified to allow the AUV to autonomously determine if it had reached the seafloor to isolate magnetometer readings at the bottom of the ocean. The sensor was calibrated to derive an equation relating the output voltage to depth by taping a pressure tube connected to the pressure sensor to a meterstick. The output voltage of the circuit was recorded while holding the end of the tube at depths from 0-0.4m in increments of 0.05m in a graduated cylinder filled with seawater. Figure X shows the resultant calibration curve with 95% confidence level upper and lower observational and functional bounds. The \(R^2\) value for the fit was 0.996. After calibration, it was noted that the maximum depth that could be recorded was 3.76m under the surface of the water, which was outside the planned 0-3m range.



Figure X. Modified Pressure Sensor Circuit Calibration Curve




Thermistor
The NXFT15XH103FEAB035 changes its resistance based on its contact temperature. From its datasheet, thermistor resistances of 95420-47000 \(\Omega\) were expected for temperatures of 10-25°C, which is the approximate ocean temperature at Dana Point in April with a 2-5°C buffer on each side. As shown in Figure X, a voltage divider was created with the thermistor to convert this output resistance to an output voltage. A unity gain buffer and offset amplifier were then used to scale this output to 0-3.3V in the same way as the pressure sensor. The voltage divider equation is \(V_{in}=\frac{5R_{div}}{R_t+R_{div}}\), with the variable values as depicted in Figure X.



Figure X. Modified Thermistor Interface Circuit


The offset amplifier was designed with an offset of 12.13V and a gain of -3. This resulted in theoretical output voltages of 0.37-2.95V for temperatures 25-10°C, which is within the desired range. Like the pressure sensor, the voltage buffer on each side of the output prevents railing out during deployment.
The output of the thermistor interface circuit is DC voltage, so the default 10Hz sampling frequency in the code was sufficient, and no software modifications were made.
The thermistor resistance is related to temperature based on the Steinhart-Hart equation, where T is the temperature in K, R is the thermistor resistance in \(\Omega\), and A, B, C, and D are unitless Steinhart-Hart coefficients. As shown in Figure X, the thermistor was calibrated by measuring output voltages when placing the thermistor in 10-25°C water baths, backcalculating the thermistor resistance using, and finding the Steinhart-Hart coefficients. The coefficients with 95% confidence bounds were found to be A=0.02348 (-0.1563, 0.2032), B=-0.005701 (-0.05414, 0.04274), C=5.159 \(\times10^{-4}\) (-0.003816, 0.004848), and D=-1.487 \(\times10^{-5}\) (-1.424×\(10^{-4}\), 1.127×\(10^{-4}\)). Combining the offset amplifier equation and Steinhart-Hart equation determined the relationship between output voltage and temperature.



Figure X. Steinhart-Hart Fit With 95% Confidence Lebel Upper and Lower Functional/Observational Bounds Relating Thermistor Resistance to Contact Temperature




Magnetometer
The magnetometer interface circuit was not modified after the I2C connection (Serial Clock (SCL), Serial Data (SDA), and Data Ready (DRDY) lines) was tested to work.
The default 10Hz sampling frequency in the code was sufficient for the magnetometer readings. The magnetic flux density was expected to be a roughly constant value at each position, and not a periodic signal, so the sampling frequency producing aliasing was not a concern. Separately, the RM3100 has a data update rate of 37Hz, meaning it would complete a measurement and flag DRDY every 0.027s [13]. If the sampling frequency were more than 37Hz, the Teensy 4.0 could attempt to read data when there is no real output, producing gaps or anomalous values in the recorded data.
Modifications to the code were made in the form of writing C++ functions and constants necessary for the magnetometer to collect and save separate-axis and total magnitude magnetic flux density readings in µT.
The sensor was re-validated before deployment by using it to collect data in open air and away from any ferromagnetic objects (apart from data collection hardware) for around 10 minutes. Figure X shows the results of this data collection, where readings fluctuated between around 50.25-50.6µT, which falls within the expected range of 22-67µT on the Earth’s surface.



Figure X. Magnetic Flux Density Readings Collected in Open Air over 10 Minutes

title: Crystal Radio Experiments
text:
Pickard Crystal Radio
I started with the Pickard Crystal Radio, because it looked the simplest. It only had a variable inductor, a capacitor, resistor and diode. Because I knew radios could be tuned to different frequencies, I assumed the variable inductor would be used for tuning. My knowledge of RLC circuits helped me understand that this circuit would resonate at a specific frequency, based on the component values. Since the inductor was variable, I could adjust the resonant frequency to match the desired broadcast frequency. I also knew the basics of diodes, so I assumed it would have to go in a specific direction in order to hear any sound. It turns out this specifically needed to be a germanium diode, as opposed to the more common silicone diodes, because of their lower forward voltage drop. This prevents the diode from absorbing too much of the signal (since the power output of the crystal radio is tiny), which would make most AM signals inaudible. Figure 1. shows the schematic I ended up using.



Figure 1. Pickard Crystal Radio Schematic

title: Crystal Radio Experiments
text:
Dunwoody Crystal Radio
The Dunwoody Crystal Radio was similar to the Pickard Crystal Radio in that it used similar components. However, it had two tuning capacitors in addition to the variable inductor. This would allow for more fine-tuning of the selected frequency. Instead of the variable inductor being adjustable by a simple conductive slider, the inductor had various coil taps that I first adjusted to select the broad operational frequency. I then adjusted the tuning capacitors to fine-tune the selected signal. Figure 2. shows the schematic of the circuit.



Figure 2. Dunwoody Crystal Radio Schematic

title: Crystal Radio Experiments
text:
Armstrong Regenerative Circuit Radio
This circuit was very different. It used a combination of inductors with a tickler coil to feed the output signal back into the circuit. It also used a triode vacuum tube to amplify the signal, which meant it needed two external power sources to work. Figure 3. shows the schematic of the circuit.



Figure 3. Armstrong Regenerative Circuit Radio Schematic


I was not able to get this circuit to work, even after replacing all components apart from the vacuum tube, which I could not find a replacement for. This led me to believe the vacuum tube was faulty.
From my research, I believe replacing the vacuum tube with a JFET (Junction Field-Effect Transistor) would be a viable next step for debugging. The vacuum tube works as an electron valve, controlling a current with a tiny input voltage. When the radio signal fluctuates slightly, the current output of the vacuum tube has large fluctuations, which is how the signal gets amplified. JFETs similarly change current flow based on input voltage.
I also think this would be a good substitution to do in general since the vacuum tube needed a really large voltage supply (45V+ battery) to run, while a JFET could function in the same way using a 9V battery. This would make the radio more accessible and cheaper to run as the setup I was using chained five 9V batteries together in series.

title: FPGA-Controlled Keypad Scanner
text:
Design and Testing Methodology
To do this, I created two submodules that were linked by a top-level module. The top-level module included combinational logic to convert the four switch inputs to LED on/off states, and called the two submodules and HSOSC to control the oscillating LED and 7-segment display.
One submodule controlled a counter that would “step down” the 24MHz HSOSC clock to a 2.4Hz clock. It did this by counting HSOSC rising edges until some maximum value, then inverting whatever output it generated previously. Since I set up the HSOSC to have an output frequency of 24MHz and the target frequency was 2.4Hz, I divided these to get the delay count (how many clock ticks of the 24MHz clock needed to count up to to equal one 2.4Hz clock tick).
\(\frac{24MHz}{2.4Hz} = \frac{24 \times 10^7 Hz}{2.4 Hz} = 10^7\)
Each clock cycle has a high and low state that are equal in length, and the oscillating LED should turn on when the clock is high. This means the LED should toggle twice each cycle.
So the LED would toggle every \(\frac{10^7}{2} = 5 \times 10^6\) 24MHz clock ticks.
The counter was also given a reset and enable input for additional functionality in case the submodule needs to be used in a future design. The reset, tied to a button input, resets the counter to 0 when pressed. The enable input, tied to a constant high signal from the top-level module, allows the counter to run as expected when high and hold its current value when low. When the counter reached the maximum count value, it reset to 0 and inverted the output signal. This would act as the on-board LED toggle.
The other submodule implemented the combinational logic to control the 7-segment display based on the 4 switch inputs. Because of the large number of output signals, the combinational logic was implemented using a case statement instead of a series of implied logic gates.
The design was tested using waveform simulation of the top-level module and each submodule in QuestaSim through automatic testbenches to confirm the desired behaviour.
The counter submodule testbench instantiated the submodule freqconverter (with parameters WIDTH and MAX set to 4 and 10 respectively) under a test and generated a clock signal with a cycle time of 2ns. To start testing, enable and reset were first toggled so they were high. Then, the output signal was checked at every MAX number of clock signals to confirm the desired ON/OFF frequency. The reset was then toggled after a small delay and the output signal was checked again with the same intervals to confirm the reset put the counter value back at 0. The enable was then set to low and the same tests were performed to confirm the counter stopped running when enable was low.
The 7-segment display submodule testbench instantiated the submodule switch_7seg under a test, then went through each combination of four switch inputs while checking the seven segments were outputting the correct values.
The top-level module was tested in three separate testbenches. First was a testbench to test the clock generated by the HSOSC. The top-level output clk signal was checked at the time it takes to complete half a 24MHz clock cycle twice to confirm the signal is oscillating high/low at the 24MHz.
Another testbench was written to test the combinational logic of the on-board LEDs and the connection to the 7-segment submodule. Similar to the 7-segment display submodule testbench, this testbench instantiated the top-level module lab1_nk under a test, then went through each combination of four switch inputs while checking the on-board LEDs were outputting the correct values and the seven segments were being mapped to the top-level seven segment outputs.
The final top-level testbench tested the connection to the counter submodule. After instantiating the top-level module lab1_nk under a test, the reset signal was toggled high, and the oscillating LED signal was checked every half stepped-down clock signal to confirm the submodule output signal was oscillated at the right frequency and being mapped to the LED. The reset signal was toggled after a small delay and the oscillating LED signal was checked at the same interval to confirm the reset put the counter back at 0 and did not affect the signal mapping.
Finally, the 7-segment display circuit was built and connected to the FPGA GPIO pins, and the full design was uploaded to the FPGA and deployed on the hardware. The design was tested by toggling the switches to account for all cases and observing the LED and 7-segment display outputs to confirm functionality, as well as probing the output oscillating signal with an oscilloscope to confirm its frequency is 2.4Hz.
To implement this design on hardware, the GPIO pins needed to be connected to current-limiting resistors before the 7-segment display diodes. The common anode of the 7-segment display was connected to 3.3V and the forward voltage of each diode within the display is 2V. I provided 5-20mA to each diode to ensure proper operation. Using Ohm’s Law,



\[
\begin{aligned}
V&=IR\\
V_s-V_{fw}&=I_{min}R_{max}\\
3.3-2&=0.005R_{max}\\
R_{max}&=260\Omega
\end{aligned}
\]


\[
\begin{aligned}
V&=IR\\
V_s-V_{fw}&=I_{max}R_{min}\\
3.3-2&=0.005R_{min}\\
R_{min}&=65\Omega
\end{aligned}
\]



Picking a value in between 65Ω and 260Ω would yield 5-20mA, so using what was available I chose 150Ω resistors.

title: FPGA-Controlled Keypad Scanner
text:
Design and Testing Methodology
I created two submodules and linked them by a top-level module.
The first submodule called the counter module from before to step down a 24MHz HSOSC clock to a 120Hz clock. Based on the positive edge of the new clock signal, it would change which anode output (left vs right side) would be tied high, which determines which 7-segment side to write to. 120Hz was chosen because based on trial and error, this frequency allowed both segments to be perceived as on at the same time without any flickering or bleeding.
The second submodule called the counter module from before to step down a 24MHz HSOSC clock to a 1Hz clock. It then used assign statements to change each bit of the keypad row scanning output, so that only 1 bit out of 4 would be high at a time and they would oscillate at a rate of 2Hz.
The top-level module called on the two submodules and HSOSC. The anode output was connected as the select of a 2:1 mux, so that it’s value determined which set of switches would be fed into the 7-segment submodule and the correct 7-segment pattern can be written. The column inputs were inverted and written to LEDs the LEDs blink at 2Hz when the corresponding row is scanned and column is pressed.
The design was tested using waveform simulation of the top-level module and the scanning submodule in QuestaSim through automatic testbenches to confirm the desired behaviour.
The scanning submodule testbench instantiated the submodule scan under a test. Reset and enable were pulled high. The row outputs were then checked every 0.006s as this is how long it should take for them to toggle. The reset was then pulled low and high and the row outputs were checked to reset to 4’b1000 and start rotating. Then, enable was set to low to confirm the row outputs would stop rotating, and reset was pulled high again to check the row outputs reset and did not continue changing.
The top-level submodule testbench instantiated the module lab_nk under a test. Reset was set high, switch inputs were set and the segments were checked after 8333334ns to confirm that the left/right segments were only written at the corresponding anode values. Then, different column inputs were written and the led outputs were checked to confirm the led bits were inverted column bits.
The dual 7-segment display circuit and keypad scanner circuit were built and connected separately to the FPGA GPIO pins because there were not enough pins to connect all the inputs and outputs at the same time. The design was tested by toggling all 8 switch inputs and observing the 7-segment display outputs, and then pressing keypad buttons individually and multiple in the same row/column and observing the LED outputs.
To implement this in hardware, PNP transistors need to be wired to the anodes of the dual 7-segment display because the required current is greater than what the FPGA GPIO pins can drive and NPN transistors need to be wired to the rows of the 4x4 keypad to prevent shorting multiple row drivers when multiple keys are pressed (functioning as an open-drain/collector output).
PNP transistors have a base-emitter saturation voltage of about 0.7V. Since I supplied the emitter with 3.3V, the voltage at the base would be \(V_B=3.3V-0.7V=2.6V\). The transistor is active when the base is low, so current will flow when the GPIO pin is low (0V). Also, the collector-emitter saturation voltage is about 0.25V, so the voltage at the collector would be \(V_C=3.3V-0.25V=3.05V\). Additionally, the forward voltage of an LED is around 2V. The maximum current the GPIO pins can handle is 8mA, so using Ohm’s law,



\[
\begin{aligned}
V&=IR\\
V_B-V_{GPIO}&=I_{B}R_{B}\\
2.6-0&=0.008R_{B}\\
R_{B}&=325\Omega
\end{aligned}
\]


\[
\begin{aligned}
V&=IR\\
V_C-V_{LED}&=I_{pin}R_{C}\\
3.05-2&=0.008R_{C}\\
R_{C}&=131.25\Omega
\end{aligned}
\]





Figure 13. PNP Transistor Circuit





From these calculations, I used a 330Ω resistor for the base because it is slightly higher than the calculated value, which would prevent drawing too much current from the FPGA. I used a 150Ω resistor for the collector using this same logic.
Similarly, NPN transistors have a base-emitter voltage of around 0.7V. Since I supplied the emitter with 0V, the voltage at the base would be \(V_B=0.7V-0V=0.7V\). The transistor is active when the base is high, so current will flow when the GPIO pin is low (3.3V). The maximum current the GPIO pins can handle is 8mA, so using Ohm’s law,



\[
\begin{aligned}
V&=IR\\
V_GPIO-V_{B}&=I_{B}R_{B}\\
3.3-0.7&=0.008R_{B}\\
R_{B}&=325\Omega
\end{aligned}
\]


\[
\]





Figure 14. NPN Transistor Circuit





With this I chose a 330Ω resistor for the base because it is slightly higher than the calculated value, which would prevent drawing too much current from the FPGA.
The keypad-driven LEDs also needed current-limiting resistors since the maximum current the LEDs could handle was 20mA. They also had a forward voltage of about 2.2V, so using Ohm’s law,
\[
\begin{aligned}
V&=IR\\
3.3-2.2&=0.02R\\
R&=55\Omega
\end{aligned}
\]
This was the minimum current-limiting resistor needed, so I chose a 330Ω resistor.

title: FPGA-Controlled Keypad Scanner
text:
Design and Testing Methodology
This design was achieved using a finite state machine (see Figures 24 and 25), where the state would change depending on the collected key inputs. The variable keyMap is the current key inputs, while initialKeyMap is a snapshot of the key inputs during the display state. In the display state, displayEN is set high, which allows writing to the 7 segment display through flip-flops in the top-level module.



Figure 24. State transition diagram for the finite state machine





Figure 25. State transition table for the finite state machine


Like in the previous phase, key inputs were determined by “scanning” each row (sending a high bit to one row at a time) and collecting the column inputs. The column inputs were sent through a synchronizer to prevent reading metastable values. Besides the scan module, a keyMap module was developed to convert the corresponding row/column combination to a 16-bit key map.
The keypad switches were prone to switch bounce (the switch makes and breaks its connection repeatedly for up to ~10ms). To mitigate this issue and ensure each key was only registered once, a debouncer submodule was created, which used a shift register to compare the keymap at different intervals and only register the keys when all registers had the same value.
This debounced key map was an input to the FSM, a submodule converting the keys to equivalent switch inputs (which were sent into the 7-segment decoder).
The top level module wired all these submodules together, and had assign statements to compare counter values to provide the switching frequency for the 7-segment anodes, as well as a mux to determine which value to write to the left and right segments.
These modules were all tested using automatic testbenches, waveform simulation, and hardware deployment.
I think my debouncing strategy is more accurate and time efficient than other strategies. One other strategy I can think of is just waiting 10ms (maximum bouncing time) after the first button press before using the keyMap. However, this doesn’t guarantee that after you wait, the button is actually debounced - it could slightly fluctuate, or if your count is off by a little bit you would read and use the bounce. Adding a strategy of storing the initial read and comparing at the end of the wait time to confirm debouncing could work. However, if another button happens to activate during the 10ms wait time, that button could still bounce after the first button is done, so then you would have to wait again. Using the shift register method means you don’t have to have logic determining the first key press, or wait a specified amount of time. You always read until all registers log the same value.
However, the other strategies are probably more hardware efficient as I do use 9 flip-flops (probably could’ve used less, I was just being cautious), whereas the waiting strategy would just rely on a counter output that uses 1 flip-flop.
My design technically includes 2 communicating FSMs that evaluates the current debounced keyMap against the saved keyMap. I think another way to do achieve the end goal (with the alternative debouncing strategies described above) is to have a canonical FSM managing the display/scanning states communicate with another canonical FSM to control whether debouncing is active or not, or communicate with a non-canonical FSM which is a counter to keep track of how long to wait for. However, I think this is more complicated and could make the overal FSM structure less reliable since switching or keeping states depend on more conditions that could be unexpected values right when the clock edge occurs, meaning you have to wait for the next cycle to actually transition correctly.

title: Leverging MCU Interrupts to Read Stepper Motor Encoders
text:
Introduction
In this lab, a design was implemented on the MCU to accurately determine the speed and direction of a stepper motor through encoder outputs.

title: Leverging MCU Interrupts to Read Stepper Motor Encoders
text:
Design and Testing Methodology
The stepper motor has two quadrature encoders with one hall effect sensor each. The sensors are 90° out of phase. To design this implementation, two interrupts were configured to activate at the rising and falling edge of each sensor input. Figure 1 shows a flow chart of the main program and its communications with the interrupt handlers.



Figure 1. Flow chart of the implementation


Using the collected pin readings, the direction of the motor spin was derived within each interrupt. This was done to maximize the accuracy of the direction at any point in time. The direction derivation logic is shown in Figure 2.



Figure 2. Motor direction logic


During each interrupt, a count was also incremented. Since the motor has 408 pulses per revolution, Our counter reaches 4*408 every time the motor completes one revolution. The speed (in revolutions per second) was calculated per Figure 3.



Figure 3. Motor speed calculation


The implementation also utilizes a timer to print out the speed and direction at 1Hz. The timer internal clock was configured to run at 10kHz, and when the timer count reached 10000, the speed and direction would print, and then the speed count and print count would both be reset.
Interrupts are the better option compared to manual polling at high speeds, because with this setup, you never miss a rising and falling edge, whereas the polling intervals may not be fine enough, leading to missed edges. Furthermore, polling doesn’t guarantee we sample at a rising or falling edge, and we are relying on the fact that the two encoder sensors are 90° out of phase. With manual polling, you could sample within the high/low region of either signal incorrectly assume counterclockwise/clockwise motion. If we spin the motor at its maximum theoretical speed of 2.5rev/s, we would need a minimum polling frequency of 4080Hz to accurately capture all pulses (since A and B are 90° out of phase, there are 408 pulses per revolution, and we want 4 samples per pulse). However, the polling frequency needed to accurately measure the motor speed and direction would change as the motor speed changes, because you would be sampling at not clock edge times. Therefore, using interrupts are better.
One possible tradeoff is that when you use interrupts, everything on the MCU CPU stops running, whereas with polling, nothing stops running while data is being taken. So polling can take samples continuously no matter what, whereas if the interrupt is very long, you might miss signals. However, in our case our interrupt is extremely short, so this effect is negligible.

text:
Underwater Acoustics and Fast Fourier Transforms
Acoustics are helpful for a variety of sensors, such as sonar and radar. To investigate the feasibility of underwater acoustic measurements, the team used acoustic measurements to locate the position of the proto-AUV in a tank with multiple speakers emitting set frequencies.

Getting Familiar With Signal Processing Using
Fast Fourier Transforms were applied using the FFT function of an oscilloscope to 11kHz and 12kHz sine and square waves with 1.5V amplitude and 0V offset.






Figure Xa. 11kHz, 1.5V Amplitude, 0V Offset Sine Wave With FFT







Figure Xb. 12kHz, 1.5V Amplitude, 0V Offset Sine Wave With FFT









Figure Xc. 11kHz, 1.5V Amplitude, 0V Offset Square Wave With FFT







Figure Xd. 11kHz, 1.5V Amplitude, 0V Offset Square Wave With Hanning Window and FFT








Figure Xe. MATLAB Plot of the Frequency Spectrum of the 11kHz, 1.5V Amplitude, 0V Offset Square Wave With Hanning Window


The plots of FFT magnitude show the amplitude of frequencies in the signal. Since Figure Xa shows a 11kHz sine wave and its FFT, we see a single peak at 11kHz, whereas Figure Xb shows a 12kHz sine wave and its FFT, so we see a single peak at 12kHz.
Figure Xc shows a 11kHz square wave and its FFT, and since a square wave can be represented by the sum of sine waves with odd integer multiples of frequencies, we see multiple peaks, each at an odd integer multiple of 11kHz.






NoteExpand for the square wave/sum of sine waves with odd integer multiples of frequencies derivation





The unit step function is given by: \[
\begin{aligned}
U(x)&=0 \text{ (for }x<0)\\
U(x)&=\frac{1}{2} \text{ (for }x=0)\\
U(x)&=1 \text{ (for }x>0)\\
\end{aligned}
\]
A square wave with period \(T=2L\) can be expressed as \(f(t)=2(U(\frac{t}{L})-U(\frac{t}{L}-1))-1\).
The Fourier Series representation of this signal is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(t)&=a_0+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}a_kcos(kw_ot)+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}b_kcos(kw_ot)\\
&=a_0+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}a_kcos(k\frac{\pi}{L}t)+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}b_kcos(k\frac{\pi}{L}t)\\
\end{aligned}
\]
Since the square wave is an odd function, \(a_o=a_k=0\). Solving for \(b_k\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_k&=\frac{2}{T}\int_{0}^{T}f(t)sin(k\frac{\pi}{L}t)dt\\
&=\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{2L}f(t)sin(k\frac{\pi}{L}t)dt\\
&=\frac{2}{n\pi}(1-(-1)^n)\\
\end{aligned}
\]
Which gives \(b_k=\frac{4}{n\pi}\) for odd integers k or \(b_k=0\) for even integers k.
Therefore, the sum of sines representation of a square wave is \(f(t)=\sum_{n=1,3,5,...}^{\infty}\frac{4}{n\pi}sin(2\pi nft)\).



Since n is a positive odd integer, and we take the sum of the function from n to infinity, the frequency peak locations would be equal to nf = positive odd integer multiples of 11kHz. This is why we see them present at 11, 33, 55, 77, 99 kHz (the x-axis only goes up to 105Hz). If the x-axis extended further, the magnitude of the peaks would eventually become so small that we wouldn’t be able to see them anyway. As more n-terms (and thus frequencies) are included, the sum of sines representation of the square wave gets closer to the shape of a perfect square wave.
Figure Xd also shows a 11kHz square wave, but with a Hanning window applied, and this eliminates the peaks at the non-odd integer multiples of 11kHz due to the Hanning window removing the periodic discontinuities and additional sinusoid component additions to compensate for them.
Figure Xe shows a MATLAB-generated plot of the frequency spectrum of the same signal in Figure Xd. The FFT peak positions match between Figures Xe and Xd, but the magnitude of the peaks is different because the y-axis of the oscilloscope plot is in decibels, while the y-axis of the MATLAB plot is in volts.
Fourier transformations expect all data that is put into it to be periodic, but the collected data is unlikely to be cut off at exactly a period of the real signal, so after the Fourier transform extends the collected data by repeating what is given to it, the FFT algorithm will think there is a periodic discontinuity and add a bunch of high frequency sinusoids to account for the mismatch. Multiplying the data by a windowing function makes sure the data goes to 0 at the sides of the window, and this removes any periodic discontinuities when the signal is repeated. Using a rectangular window would be like using no window at all since the whole signal is multiplied by a constant, so it has an assumed periodic discontinuity, and the Fourier transform will add many high-frequency sinusoids to compensate, whereas using a Hanning window would make the data at the sides of the window go to 0, removing the need for these undesired sinusoids.
